title: Mendelian inheritance does not by itself change allele frequencies
body: G. H. Hardy's 1908 letter in Science, "Mendelian Proportions in a Mixed Population," answers a confusion about Mendelian inheritance. In a large population where mates pair at random, one round of Mendelian inheritance puts genotype frequencies into a definite relation to allele frequencies. Those frequencies then stay put. Mendelian segregation alone does not drive a dominant allele to take over, and it does not remove recessive alleles. Change in the frequencies requires something else: selection, migration, mutation, non-random mating, or chance in a small population. The relation is often called Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium because Wilhelm Weinberg published a similar argument the same year. Weinberg's paper is not linked here, so this card rests on Hardy.
